content: Greater burdock, also known as edible burdock or Lappa burdock, is a biennial plant belonging to the Arctium genus within the Asteraceae family. It is cultivated in gardens primarily for its root, which is used as a vegetable. This plant can grow to a height of up to 2 meters. Its leaves are large, alternate, and heart-shaped (cordiform), with long petioles. The underside of the leaves is covered in fine hairs (pubescent). The flowers are purple and grouped into spherical flower heads (capitula), which are clustered together. These flowers typically bloom in mid-summer. The capitula are surrounded by an involucre composed of numerous bracts, each of which curves into a hook. This unique structure allows the flower heads to attach to the fur of animals, facilitating long-distance dispersal. The fruits of greater burdock are achenes, which are elongated, compressed, and have short pappuses. The plant’s fleshy taproot can grow as long as 1 meter. Greater burdock is native to temperate regions of the Old World, ranging from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean, and from the British Isles through Russia, the Middle East, China, and Japan, including parts of India. It has become naturalized in many regions worldwide and is commonly found in disturbed areas, particularly in nitrogen-rich soils. In Japan, it is widely cultivated and has even lent its name to a specific construction technique known as burdock piling. This plant thrives in fresh, well-worked soil that is rich in humus and requires full sunlight for optimal growth. It is highly responsive to nitrogen-based fertilizers. Propagation is achieved by directly sowing seeds in mid-summer. The roots are typically harvested three to four months after sowing, up until late autumn, as they become too fibrous if left in the ground for longer. In traditional medicine, dried burdock is regarded by herbalists as a diuretic, a diaphoretic (promoting sweating), and an agent for purifying the blood.
